title: Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals
description:
# Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals

Given a data stream of non-negative integers, summarize the values seen so far as a sorted list of disjoint closed intervals.

Implement the `SummaryRanges` class:

*   `SummaryRanges()` initializes an empty stream.
*   `void addNum(int value)` adds `value` to the stream. Adding the same value more than once must not change the summary.
*   `int[][] getIntervals()` returns the current summary as disjoint intervals `[starti, endi]`, sorted by `starti`.

The stream contains individual values, not counts. If values `1`, `2`, and `3` have appeared, they must be returned as one interval `[1, 3]`. If a newly inserted value connects two existing intervals, the two intervals and the new value must merge into one interval.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["SummaryRanges", "addNum", "getIntervals", "addNum", "getIntervals", "addNum", "getIntervals", "addNum", "getIntervals", "addNum", "getIntervals"]
[[], [1], [], [3], [], [7], [], [2], [], [6], []]
**Output**
[null, null, [[1, 1]], null, [[1, 1], [3, 3]], null, [[1, 1], [3, 3], [7, 7]], null, [[1, 3], [7, 7]], null, [[1, 3], [6, 7]]]

**Explanation**
After adding `1`, `3`, and `7`, the stream has three separate intervals. Adding `2` bridges `[1, 1]` and `[3, 3]` into `[1, 3]`. Adding `6` extends the interval `[7, 7]` to `[6, 7]`.

## Constraints:

*   `0 <= value <= 10^4`
*   At most `3 * 10^4` calls will be made to `addNum` and `getIntervals`.

solutions.name: TreeMap Interval Merge
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log k) per addNum, O(k) per getIntervals
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store each current interval in a `TreeMap` keyed by its start. To add a value, find the interval with the greatest start not larger than the value and the first interval starting after the value. The value is either already covered, extends the left interval, extends the right interval, bridges both, or creates a new interval.

## Key Insight

Only the immediate left and right intervals can be affected by a single inserted value. All other intervals are separated by at least one missing value and remain unchanged.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log k) for `addNum`, where `k` is the number of current intervals. `getIntervals` is O(k).
- Space Complexity: O(k), because only interval endpoints are stored.

solutions.name: Bounded BitSet Scan
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) per addNum, O(U) worst-case per getIntervals
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the bound `0 <= value <= 10^4`. Mark each inserted value in a `BitSet`. `getIntervals` jumps from one set bit to the next and uses the next clear bit to close each run.

## Key Insight

The value domain is small and fixed, so this solution trades interval-level updates for very simple writes and predictable scans. It is a useful baseline for bounded-domain design questions.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(1) for `addNum`; `getIntervals` is O(U) in the worst case, where `U = 10001`.
- Space Complexity: O(U), for the bit set.

solutions.name: TreeSet Value Scan
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per addNum, O(n) per getIntervals
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store every distinct inserted value in a `TreeSet`. Duplicates disappear automatically. To answer a query, scan values in sorted order and group consecutive runs into intervals.

## Key Insight

This route separates update correctness from interval merging. The set maintains sorted unique values, and interval construction becomes a straightforward scan over consecutive integers.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n) for `addNum`, and O(n) for `getIntervals`, where `n` is the number of distinct inserted values.
- Space Complexity: O(n), because every distinct value is stored.

solutions.name: Boundary Maps with Ordered Starts
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log k) per addNum, O(k) per getIntervals
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain three structures: a set of values already seen, a map from interval start to end, and a map from interval end to start. A sorted set of starts gives ordered output. When adding `value`, check whether an interval ends at `value - 1` and whether another starts at `value + 1`, then merge the matching boundaries.

## Key Insight

The only information needed for merging is at interval boundaries. This implementation avoids floor and ceiling interval searches by asking direct boundary questions: is there a left neighbor interval, and is there a right neighbor interval?

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log k) for `addNum` because starts are inserted and removed from a sorted set; `getIntervals` is O(k).
- Space Complexity: O(n), for seen values and interval boundary maps.

solutions.name: Disjoint Set Components
solutions.timeComplexity: O(alpha(U) + log k) per addNum, O(k) per getIntervals
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat every value as a node in a bounded disjoint-set structure. When a new value appears, activate it and union it with active neighbors `value - 1` and `value + 1`. A `TreeMap` from component start to root keeps the intervals sorted.

## Key Insight

Intervals are connected components in the graph where adjacent integers are connected. Union-find makes the merging operation explicit and is a useful way to reason about the same invariant from a graph perspective.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: almost O(1) amortized for union-find work plus O(log k) to update the sorted component map. `getIntervals` is O(k).
- Space Complexity: O(U), where `U = 10001`, for the bounded arrays.

initial query is empty and value zero is accepted
duplicate values do not create duplicate intervals
new value bridges left and right intervals
unordered insertions still return sorted intervals
both domain endpoints are handled and can be extended
duplicates inside an existing interval do not mutate state
left extension followed by bridge merge
single inserted value bridges two one-point intervals
two additions progressively merge alternating gaps
repeated queries do not change state
